title: EA creation advice?
author: Different-Team6219
selftext:
I have tried creating multiple EAs with not much success. Backtesting is marginally profitable over some periods but not over others. 

I must preface:  
\-I am not an expert trader.  
\-my coding experience is dross (I don’t feel this is the problem though with AI help)  
\-I have only been trying for 3 months or so.

From people who are experienced in the field I would like to know a few things:

\-do you need to be a successful trader first and EA creator second?  
\- As a beginner what is/are the best strategies (e.g breakout)?  
\-and in this strategy what are key components/prompts that separate unprofitable vs profitable?

I attempt to improve my EA’s through asking AI’s advice from showing backtesting results. 

\-Is it better to understand and execute a trading strategy first and then create an EA around it?  
\-are the improvements that AI offers of any actual use because they often produce poorer results?  
\-finally is there any point in creating my own or am I better off saving up and purchasing an EA?

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body:
you were the one asking about Pat's bot an hour ago, so this answers both. the line "works over some periods but not others" is the whole diagnosis: the EA has learned the periods, not the market. and the loop you describe, showing an AI the results and asking it to improve them, makes that worse every pass, because the AI is tuning to the same data you are grading on. it will always find a change that lifts the number, and it will always be a change that only lifts that number.

the fix is boring. split your history into a part the AI is allowed to see and a part nobody touches. build on the first, then run the finished rule on the second exactly once. if it dies there, it was never alive.

to your other questions: you do not need to be a good discretionary trader first, but you do need one rule you can write in a sentence before any code exists. breakout is fine as that sentence. and buying an EA does not skip any of this, it just means someone else did the tuning and charged you for it.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: good luck with it. run the holdout once and write down what it said before you touch anything.

comments.author: profittoinvest
comments.body:
We built our system from market experience, chart reading and understanding how different indicators behave. I honestly couldn’t tell you how many versions we went through before it started behaving the way we wanted.

What helped most was not asking AI to “make the strategy better”, but using backtests to find the periods where the system struggled. Then we went back to those exact periods, compared market conditions, indicators and timeframes, and looked for common characteristics behind the drawdowns and losing clusters.

Change one idea, backtest again, then forward/live test it. Repeat.

We also pushed historical testing back to 2020 so the strategy had to survive very different market regimes, not just the conditions it was developed in.

AI is extremely useful for analyzing large amounts of backtest data, comparing periods and helping you investigate why something happened. But I wouldn’t let it blindly optimize the strategy for you. You still need to decide what makes sense from a market perspective.

It’s slow and repetitive work, but if you keep narrowing down the weaknesses instead of chasing the highest backtest number, eventually the system starts becoming much more robust.

replies.author: Different-Team6219
replies.body: This is very helpful thank you.

replies.author: profittoinvest
replies.body: Glad it helped. Good luck with the testing 👍

comments.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
comments.body:
Yes, understand the strategy first and code it second. An EA is just a rulebook, so if you can't state in one sentence why the edge should exist (who's on the other side and why they lose), the code can't supply it.

On the AI part: feeding backtest results to an AI and asking it to improve them is curve-fitting with extra steps. That's why the "improvements" often look great in-sample and then die. Use AI to write and debug code, not to tune parameters.

What separates profitable from unprofitable is mostly process:

* Split your data. Develop on one period, then test once on a period you never touched. Better still, forward test on demo for a few hundred trades.
* Include spread, slippage, and commission. Many marginal EAs turn negative after costs.
* Keep parameters few. If tiny changes to the inputs flip the result, there's no edge.
* Check by regime. "Profitable in some periods, not others" usually means it depends on volatility or session, or gets hit around news.

That last one is often fixable with a filter. Stand the EA down around high-impact releases (CPI, NFP, rate decisions) and see if the equity curve smooths out. EventTrader has pre-tagged event timing for this, or you can use any clean calendar, as long as the timestamps are point-in-time.

Buying an EA: mostly no. If it had a real edge, the seller would trade it rather than sell it. Ask for a live, third-party-verified track record, not backtests.
